title: Analysis of TME-microbe spatial relationship and gene expression to predict recurrence in oral squamous cell carcinoma
text:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a prevalent cancer with high recurrence rates and poor survival outcomes, and
current staging systems fail to accurately predict patient prognosis. This project aims to identify how the
microbiome and intra-tumoral bacteria influence the tumor microenvironment and will utilize multi-omics
integration to develop a predictive tool for recurrence-free survival. The resulting biomarker panel will enhance
risk stratification, guide treatment choices, and inform the development of new microbiome- and immune-
targeted therapies to improve survival rates in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma.

title: Molecular mechanisms governing selective autophagy in mammalian cells
text:
The dysregulation of autophagy is associated with cancer, neurodegeneration and aging, but the mechanistic
details behind these relationships are poorly understood. The proposed research will elucidate the role of
autophagy receptors in selective autophagy, focusing on the mechanism(s) by which receptors identify
potentially toxic structures and induce their degradation. A thorough understanding of autophagy mechanisms
will inform our understanding of how autophagy becomes dysregulated in disease and guide therapeutic
attempts to ameliorate these deficiencies.

title: Multidimensional Sleep Health in Adolescents: Social Determinants and Biological Consequences
text:
This research advances fundamental knowledge of how social environments shape adolescent sleep and how
poor sleep contributes to physiological dysregulation associated with chronic disease risk. By identifying
modifiable social determinants and biobehavioral pathways, my F31 project can inform targeted interventions
to improve sleep health during adolescence, a critical developmental period. Ultimately, this F31 work aims to
enhance lifelong health, reduce early disease risk, and address public health priorities related to adolescent
sleep.

title: Circulating Biomarkers and Imaging for Early Detection of Pancreatic Cancer
text:
This renewal application proposes to validate early detection biomarker signatures comprising of pathway
associated circulating transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics (omics) biomarkers and integrate them
with machine learning method derived high resolution imaging features associated with heterogenous pancreatic
ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) disease subtypes. Integration of Omics data with CT/MRI imaging features will
be done by developing Multimodal Integrative Analytical Models (MIAM) predictive of early stage pancreatic
cancer. Validation of the integrated biomarker signatures and their association with PDAC subtypes will be
investigated in Phases II, III and IV studies according to PRoBE-design while performance in phase IV study for
detecting early stage disease and predicting clinical outcomes among asymptomatic patients and at-risk
individuals will be ascertained with retrospective and prospective longitudinal pre-diagnostic sample cohorts,
including one representing an underserved population.

title: Advancing immune organoid technology and organoid combinations
text: We have assembled a broad and highly accomplished team to continue our investigations of Influenza and SARS-CoV-2 vaccination and infection, particular focusing on subjects that are vulnerable and seeking a deeper understanding of the effects of specific antibody glycosylation and specificity, bioinformatic signatures of pan virus responses and human immune organoids and the tissues and organs they interact with.

title: Training/Dissemination-Resource for Molecular Imaging Agents in Precision Medicine
text: TRAINING AND DISSEMINATION SUMMARY We consider the NCBIB to be primarily about dissemination of our technology. The most important kind of dissemination is training that we can provide not only to individuals in the molecular imaging community, but also to those involved in the allied health sciences and other areas of STEM. We have significantly enhanced both the training and dissemination aspects of the NCBIB in this renewal application. In terms of training, we intend to reach out more actively to students in the community. A second innovation in education and training is to link our NCBIB to two other imaging-centric NCBIBs, one at Washington University and the other at Harvard/MGH, whereby we will not only share reagents but also speakers at our webinars and symposia. We will co-sponsor more educational activities than in the past, having recently established formal ties to programs at the annual meeting of the World Molecular Imaging Society. Dissemination has been enhanced through closer ties to large pharma and equipment manufacturers, as well as through founding our own start-up companies, one dedicated to molecular imaging and theranostic agents and the other to developing artificial intelligence solutions to issues in molecular imaging and therapy. That latter company, an outgrowth from the Informatics Core in the Division of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging at Johns Hopkins, will help to produce software that can be downloaded from our website by interested parties. We have come to recognize that by partnering with industry we can perform or be involved in the kinds of studies necessary to advance a product to FDA approval, and its attendant widespread dissemination. Education in entrepreneurship is another new aspect to this core. The aforementioned activities will occur in concert with the usual means of dissemination, including publication in peer-reviewed journals, book chapters, invited lectures and other media. Because we generate clinical agents, we will also provide materials, protocols and IND cross-references when requested, and through material transfer agreements, if necessary. We have also learned the importance of one-on-one training, with the leaders of this core contributing many hours in this fashion, not only for disseminating our domain expertise but also as a recruitment tool to the NCBIB.

title: Cancer Immunoprevention Network (CIP-Net) Resource Coordinating Center
text:
Despite advances in immunoprevention for virus-associated cancers, preventing cancers not
caused by infectious agents remains a significant challenge. The goal of our proposed Data and Resource
Coordinating Center (DRCC) application is to catalyze collaboration across the Cancer Immunoprevention
Network (CIP-Net) and to manage, integrate and disseminate the data and resources generated through the
network. By leveraging cutting-edge, multidisciplinary team approaches, we will support CIP-Net in fostering a
collaborative community of cancer immunoprevention researchers, collectively working to understand the basic
mechanisms of immunoprevention, discover novel immunoprevention strategies, and develop and test
preclinical interventions.

title: Novel Incidental Calcium Evaluation (NICE)
text:
Modified Public Health Relevance/Narrative Section
This study will evaluate and refine an artificial intelligence computer program (an
“algorithm”) that can quickly read thousands of CT scans to look for calcium deposits in
heart arteries to better predict heart attacks, strokes, and death. The study will also hold
focus groups to identify the best way for patients and their doctors to use the information
from the algorithm to initiate treatment for heart disease prevention. If the algorithm works
as expected, it could be used to automatically screen millions of patients who are unaware
of their risk for heart disease and guide them toward lifesaving treatment.

title: Therapeutic Inhibition of MYC:TRRAP Interaction in Cancer
text:
The goal of this project is to develop new cancer therapeutics that work by blocking the activity of the MYC
oncogene. We have developed a revolutionary drug discovery platform that, for the first time, has enabled the
screening and identification of promising small molecules that directly inhibit the cancer-promoting function of
MYC. We will perform a series of in vitro and in vivo assessment of these hits to determine their suitability for
progression towards a clinically relevant, novel, highly MYC-specific, and safe cancer therapy, which currently
does not exist.

title: Cell-lineage specific epigenomic determinants of HIV latency in humanized mouse brain and blood
text:
HIV infection of microglial cells in the brain causes HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder and represents a
viral reservoir that is a barrier to cure the infection. This study exploits a novel experimental model system where
primary human microglial cells and immune cells are xenografted into mice and altered to carry a genetic reporter
system to identify actively and latently HIV-infected cells. The system will illuminate at single cell resolution the
transcriptomics, epigenomics, and 3D genomic state of the HIV infected cells in the brain in response to
antiretroviral treatment and after treatment with latency reversal agents.

title: A commercialized platform for diversified large-scale chronic electrophysiology
text:
This project aims to develop and commercialize an integrated circuit that can amplify and digitize
512 concurrent neural signals from multi-channel electrode arrays. Furthermore, we aim to
develop and commercialize electronics that control multiple EChips at once and log the data to
an SD card, offering a way to scale channel counts to above 2000 without the need for cables
between the animal and a computer.

title: Enteric Glia is New Biological Target to Block Drug Resistance in Colon Cancer
text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE/PUBLIC HEALTH RELEVANCE STATEMENT
 The abysmal survival rate of patients with advanced colon cancer is attributable to resistance to
chemotherapies that have been designed to efficiently stop proliferation and initiate apoptosis in cancer cells,
but fail to appreciate the pro-chemoresistance signals emanating from cells surrounding the tumor. Proposed
studies will explore the impact of enteric glial cells, which form a dense network infiltrating colon
adenocarcinomas, and yet have been understudied in colon carcinogenesis, and in particular colon cancer
resistance to chemotherapies. Therefore, the outcomes of this project will not only improve our understanding of
the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving colon cancer chemoresistance but may also demonstrate the
therapeutic potential of developing strategies combining targeted therapies against enteric glial cell-derived
chemoprotective ligands and traditional chemotherapy regimens.

title: Impact of Cancer Therapy-Related Clonal Hematopoiesis on Cardiovascular Diseases
text:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of non-cancer deaths and a growing concern among cancer
survivors as advances in cancer treatment extend survival. Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential
(CHIP) has been linked to increased risks of CVD and all-cause mortality, yet its development after cancer
therapy and its impact on CVD among cancer patients remain severely understudied. This proposed study will
define how cancer therapies contribute to CHIP, evaluate the impact of therapy-related CHIP on CVD outcomes,
and develop a CVD risk stratification tool tailored for cancer survivors.

title: The NCI Community Oncology Research Program: The New Mexico NCORP
text: The New Mexico NCORP UNM based academic hub with its community partnerships commits to deliver the highest quality cancer trials (screening, prevention control, treatment and cancer care delivery) to all New Mexicans with a strong focus on improving all populations in access, care delivery and outcomes.

title: Vanderbilt Genomic Learning Health System Clinical Site
text:
Although genetic information provides an opportunity to personalize clinical care, it is not widely
used in practice. We will build a system to make genetic information a routine part of clinical
medicine, working in partnership with doctors and patients to learn and share strategies that
work best.

title: Using human iPS-derived in vitro models to study the role of HOX genes in musculo-skeletal development
text:
The goal of this project is to understand the cellular and molecular role of HOX transcription factors in the
development of the musculo-skeletal system. This knowledge is expected to help understand a variety of
genetic malformations and could shed light on the biology of cancer in humans.

title: Cell-type basis for auditory processing in the inferior colliculus
text:
In this proposed project we will investigate different cell types of the inferior colliculus (IC) that
are specified by molecular markers identified from single-nucleus RNA sequencing as well as
their spatial distribution patterns to interrogate their functional contributions to the central
auditory processing and the underlying circuit mechanisms. The study will establish
comprehensive understandings of the cellular and organizational bases for different functional
roles of the IC in auditory processing and perception, and may provide new mechanistic insights
for IC associated hearing impairments.

title: Assessing the Strength of Weak Ties
text:
A comprehensive identification of various weak interactions in proteins and evaluating their functional roles
using rapid experimental assays will lay a foundation to enhance our ability to comprehend how weak
interactions regulate protein structure and function. The proposed research is relevant to public health
because the knowledge is ultimately expected to enhance our manipulative ability to prevent aberrations and
dysregulation of the human proteome. Thus, the proposed research is relevant to the part of NIH’s mission
that pertains to seeking fundamental knowledge about the nature and behavior of living systems for the
application of the knowledge to enhance health.

title: Effects of IL-1 beta inhibition on vascular inflammation in TET2 clonal hematopoiesis
text:
Clonal hematopoiesis is a common, age-related condition which increases the risk for multiple health issues
including heart disease and cancer, with specific sub-types, such as TET2 clonal hematopoiesis, conferring
particularly high risk for heart attacks. Our clinical trial will provide critical insights as to why patients with TET2
clonal hematopoiesis have a high risk of heart attacks by examining the effects of a medication, which
modulates the immune system, on inflammation of the blood vessels and clonal hematopoiesis. Thus, our
study will inform strategies to prevent heart attacks and reduce clonal hematopoiesis among an aging
population.

title: Molecular basis of lineage plasticity in neuroendocrine bladder cancer: implications for therapeutic response
text:
A major knowledge gap in bladder cancer biology is to understand the biological nature of tumor heterogeneity,
manifested by “histology variants” at the morphological level, or “molecular subtypes” at the transcriptional level.
To recapitulate the urothelial carcinoma and neuroendocrine bladder cancer observed in human bladder cancer
patients, we generated complimentary genetically engineered mouse models with urothelial carcinoma and
neuroendocrine carcinoma morphology. The proposed research will leverage our mouse models and patient-
derived organoids/xenografts to elucidate the distinct neuroendocrine bladder cancer tumor initiation, lineage
plasticity, and treatment response of standard chemotherapy and chemo-immunotherapy.
